Markdown cell 1 --------------- # DeskTech Vision: Identify Connectors, Ports, and Cables from Images ## Module 2 Capstone Project Notebook (Student Version) **Project theme:** Build an image classifier that recognizes common tech connectors, ports, cables, or related desk objects from student-collected photos. **Recommended theme examples:** - USB-A - USB-C - HDMI - Ethernet / RJ45 - 3.5 mm audio jack - SD card - microSD adapter - Lightning cable - laptop charger types - small desk tools or adapters **Backup themes with the same workflow:** - recycled household item classifier - dice / card / board-game piece classifier - screws / nuts / bolts / washers classifier - keyboard key or keycap category classifier --- ## What you must do You must: 1. define a clear classification problem and choose your classes, 2. collect or curate a small image dataset, 3. organize the images into a folder structure for training, 4. build **one baseline custom CNN**, 5. build **one improved transfer-learning model**, 6. compare the models, 7. analyze errors with a confusion matrix and wrong predictions, 8. write a short reflection on limitations and next steps. --- ## Why this is a strong capstone This project is open-ended enough to feel personal, but constrained enough to succeed in a class setting. It also gives you a very realistic deep-learning workflow: - dataset design, - image preprocessing, - baseline modeling, - transfer learning, - evaluation, - failure analysis, - reflection. That is exactly the progression this notebook is designed to guide you through. Markdown cell 2 ---------------
Alternate Ideas/Options Building a custom image classifier is a fantastic portfolio piece because it shows end-to-end skills: data collection, cleaning, modeling, and evaluation. While the default "DeskTech" theme is great, here are several variations that stand out to recruiters by solving relatable, real-world problems: 1. Sustainability & Environment Waste Sorting Assistant: Classify images of trash into Recyclable Plastic, Paper, Compost, and Landfill. Why it's good: Shows you care about applying AI for social good. It also presents real-world challenges (crumpled paper vs. flat paper). Plant Disease Detector: Classify healthy vs. diseased leaves for common houseplants (e.g., Pothos, Snake Plant). 2. Retail & Logistics Self-Checkout Produce Classifier: Classify different types of fruits or vegetables (e.g., Fuji Apple vs. Granny Smith vs. Banana). Why it's good: This is a literal problem solved by computer vision in modern grocery stores. It demonstrates you understand business use cases. Package Type Identifier: Classify shipments as Cardboard Box, Poly mailer, or Mailing Tube. 3. Accessibility Currency Reader: Classify different coins or bills. Why it's good: Highlights an accessibility use case (helping visually impaired users). Dealing with varied lighting and worn-out coins makes for a great section in your error analysis. ASL Alphabet/Digits: Hand signs for letters A, B, C, D (using your own webcam to build the dataset). 4. Manufacturing & Quality Control Defect Detection: E.g., "Intact Screw" vs. "Stripped Screw", or "Good 3D Print" vs. "Spaghetti/Failed 3D Print". Why it's good: Quality assurance is one of the biggest industrial applications of computer vision. 5. Niche / Hobbyist (Great for conversation starters) LEGO Brick Sorter: Classify 2x2 brick vs. 2x4 brick vs. 1x1 plate. Guitar Pedal / Knob Classifier: Differentiating between standard audio dials. Portfolio Tip: Whichever domain a student chooses, the portfolio write-up should emphasize how they curated the dataset to avoid bias (e.g., "I made sure to photograph the objects on multiple different desk surfaces and under both natural and artificial light so the model wouldn't just memorize the background."). #### Some other options 1. DeskTech Vision: connector / port / cable classifier This is still my favorite. It feels practical and tech-adjacent, and students can say they built a model that recognizes USB-A, USB-C, HDMI, Ethernet, VGA, DisplayPort, and similar objects from photos. That sounds way better on a portfolio than “I classified cats and dogs.” 2. PCB / electronics component classifier Classify resistors, capacitors, LEDs, push buttons, breadboard jumpers, sensors, or Arduino-compatible modules. This looks very engineering-coded on a portfolio. 3. 3D-print defect detector Students classify prints as “clean,” “stringing,” “warping,” “layer shift,” and so on. Super portfolio-friendly because it sounds like quality assurance / manufacturing AI. 4. Recycling sorter vision model Classify cardboard, plastic bottle, metal can, glass, mixed trash. Good if they want something with environmental or civic relevance. 5. Tool or fastener recognizer Screws, nuts, bolts, washers, drill bits, screwdriver heads. Nice because it feels industrial and useful. 6. Keyboard / hardware accessory classifier Mechanical switch types, keycaps, mice, cables, adapters, webcams, chargers. Good for students who like PC hardware and want the project to feel personal. 7. Houseplant health or leaf issue classifier Healthy vs under-watered vs over-watered vs damaged vs diseased. Less unique than hardware, but still pretty portfolio-friendly if framed as “computer vision for small-scale monitoring.” The strongest portfolio framing is usually: “Built an image classifier for a niche real-world problem using PyTorch, transfer learning, augmentation, and error analysis.” What makes these look good is not just the topic — it is the extras: baseline CNN vs transfer-learning comparison confusion matrix sample misclassifications with commentary class imbalance discussion data augmentation experiment small demo function that predicts on a new uploaded image That combination makes the notebook feel like a mini applied-ML case study, not just code.
Markdown cell 3 --------------- ## How to use this notebook This notebook is intentionally written as a **guided capstone assignment**. That means: - instructions appear in markdown cells, - code cells are left mostly empty, - code cells contain **subtle hint comments**, - deeper hints are hidden in collapsible sections, - you are expected to make some design decisions yourself. ### Important Do **not** open the detailed hints right away. Try each task yourself first. A capstone is supposed to show that you can make choices, debug, and explain your work. --- ## Suggested workflow Work in this order: 1. Plan your classes and image collection strategy. 2. Gather your images. 3. Split and organize the dataset. 4. Build dataloaders. 5. Train a baseline CNN. 6. Evaluate it carefully. 7. Build an improved transfer-learning model. 8. Compare both models. 9. Analyze mistakes. 10. Reflect on what your system still struggles with. --- ## Deliverables checklist Your completed notebook should include: - [ ] a clear problem statement - [ ] at least **4 classes** - [ ] at least **50 images per class total** (**recommended:** 75+) - [ ] a **train / validation / test** split - [ ] a **baseline custom CNN** - [ ] an **improved pretrained transfer-learning model** - [ ] metrics and visualizations - [ ] a confusion matrix - [ ] example misclassifications - [ ] a final reflection If you go beyond the minimum, that is even better. Markdown cell 4 --------------- ## Recommended dataset structure This project works especially well with `torchvision.datasets.ImageFolder`, which expects images to be arranged in folders by class. A common structure is: ```text project_data/ raw/ class_1/ class_2/ class_3/ class_4/ split/ train/ class_1/ class_2/ class_3/ class_4/ val/ class_1/ class_2/ class_3/ class_4/ test/ class_1/ class_2/ class_3/ class_4/ ``` so for example: ```text project_data/ raw/ usb_c/ hdmi/ ethernet/ audio_jack/ split/ train/ usb_c/ hdmi/ ethernet/ audio_jack/ val/ usb_c/ hdmi/ ethernet/ audio_jack/ test/ usb_c/ hdmi/ ethernet/ audio_jack/ ``` ### Recommended split A good default is: - **70% train** - **15% validation** - **15% test** ### Data collection advice Try to vary: - angle, - background, - distance, - lighting, - orientation, - whether the object fills most of the frame. A model that only sees one background or one camera angle may memorize shortcuts instead of learning the object itself. Markdown cell 5 --------------- ## Part 0 — Project planning Before you write any code, fill in the project plan below. ### Planning prompts Edit this markdown cell and answer the following: 1. **Project title:** 2. **Your chosen classes (minimum 4):** 3. **Why these classes are visually distinguishable:** 4. **How you will collect or curate images:** 5. **What challenges you expect (similar shapes, lighting, reflections, clutter, etc.):** 6. **What "success" would look like for this project:** ### Recommended class design tips - Choose categories that are similar enough to be interesting, but not so similar that the task becomes impossible with a small dataset. - If two categories are extremely similar, you may need more data or tighter framing rules. - Try not to create classes that are really defined by the **background** instead of the object.
Hint — only open if you are stuck planning A good class set often has **4 to 8 categories**. Try something like: - USB-A - USB-C - HDMI - Ethernet - 3.5 mm audio jack - SD card This is a nice balance because: - the objects are real and personal, - they are visually distinct enough, - some pairs are still easy to confuse, - transfer learning should work well even with a modest dataset.
Code cell 6 ----------- # Replace this comment block with your own imports. # Suggested categories of imports: # - file/path utilities (for example: pathlib, os, shutil, random) # - numerical/data libraries (for example: numpy, pandas) # - plotting libraries (for example: matplotlib, seaborn) # - PyTorch core modules # - torch.utils.data utilities # - torchvision datasets, transforms, and pretrained models # - sklearn metrics utilities for evaluation # # Also: # - set a random seed # - optionally detect whether a GPU is available Markdown cell 7 --------------- ## Part 1 — Environment check and configuration In this section, you should prepare the notebook environment and define your main configuration values. ### What to include Your code should define: - the main data directory, - raw-data directory, - split-data directory, - class names or a way to infer them, - image size, - batch size, - number of epochs, - learning rate, - device (`cpu` or `cuda`). You may either: - hard-code these settings, or - store them in a small configuration dictionary. Using a config dictionary often makes the notebook easier to edit and compare later.
Hint — only open if you are stuck A very reasonable starting point is something like: - image size: `224` - batch size: `16` or `32` - baseline epochs: around `8` to `15` - transfer-learning epochs: around `5` to `10` - learning rate: often around `1e-3` for a simple baseline and smaller for fine-tuning Remember that Colab runtimes are limited, so choose values that are realistic.

# 🧠 Lesson 1 — LLMs vs. SLMs
Welcome! In this section we’ll clarify **Large Language Models (LLMs)** and **Small Language Models (SLMs)**, explain why model size matters, and explore the trade‑offs you encounter when choosing a model size for real projects.

Markdown cell 2
---------------
## 🔧 Colab Setup
Run the cell below to install everything used across *all* notebooks in this series. Skip if you’ve already executed it in a previous notebook session.

Code cell 3
-----------
!pip -q install --upgrade transformers accelerate bitsandbytes datasets huggingface_hub
!pip -q install --upgrade sentencepiece einops rich

Markdown cell 4
---------------
## 📘 Key Definitions

Markdown cell 5
---------------
**LLM (Large Language Model)**  
- Typically ≥ 13 B parameters (B = **Billion**).  
- Optimized for broad coverage, multilingual skills, chain‑of‑thought, etc.  
- Heavy compute & memory footprint.

**SLM (Small Language Model)**  
- Anywhere from 100 M to ~13 B parameters.  
- Faster, cheaper, often easier to fine‑tune locally.  
- May specialize (e.g., Qwen‑1.5‑0.5B excels at code‑completion in resource‑constrained settings).

### Where SLMs Excel
1. **Edge & Mobile inference**  
2. **On‑prem or air‑gapped deployments**  
3. **Low‑latency voice assistants**  
4. **Rapid experimentation / prototyping**

Markdown cell 6
---------------
## 📏 Param Count vs. Capability
Below we’ll grab configs for three models of different sizes and compare their parameter counts.

Code cell 7
-----------
from transformers import AutoConfig
models = ['meta-llama/Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct',
          'google/gemma-2b-it',
          'meta-llama/Meta-Llama-3-8B-Instruct']
for m in models:
    cfg = AutoConfig.from_pretrained(m)
    # Calculate the number of parameters manually based on the config
    if hasattr(cfg, 'num_parameters'):
      num_params = cfg.num_parameters()
    elif hasattr(cfg, 'n_params'):
      num_params = cfg.n_params
    elif hasattr(cfg, 'num_attention_heads') and hasattr(cfg, 'hidden_size') and hasattr(cfg, 'intermediate_size') and hasattr(cfg, 'vocab_size'):
        # This is a simplified calculation and might not be perfectly accurate for all models
        num_params = 2 * cfg.num_hidden_layers * cfg.hidden_size * cfg.intermediate_size + cfg.vocab_size * cfg.hidden_size
    else:
        num_params = 'N/A' # Cannot calculate parameters with available attributes

    print(f'{m:<55} → {cfg.num_hidden_layers:>2} layers, {cfg.hidden_size:>4} dim, ~{num_params:,} parameters')

Markdown cell 8
---------------
👉 **Take‑away:** doubling layers or hidden size *squares* memory usage & FLOPs! That’s why quantization and sparsity are crucial for SLMs.

import ipywidgets as widgets
from IPython.display import display
import yaml
#@title 📝 Config (edit YAML & click **Save Config**)
# from google.colab import widgets, output
random.seed(datetime.datetime.now().timestamp())
# use a random float to add variety to the prompt
varint = random.randint(0, 9999999)
random_bytes = os.urandom(16)

# Create a hash object (e.g., SHA256)
hash_object = hashlib.sha256()

# Update the hash object with the random bytes
hash_object.update(random_bytes)

# Get the hexadecimal representation of the hash
random_hash = hash_object.hexdigest()
default_cfg = {
  "model": "gpt-5.4-mini",
  "temperature": 0.8,
  "setting": "Dieselpunk sky‑pirate archipelago",
  "tone": "swashbuckling + mild horror",
  "intro":  "The wind howls across the deck as distant stormclouds gather. What do you do?",
  "family_safe": True,
  "max_images":10,
  "pc": {
      "name": "Captain Aella",
      "species": "Augmented Human",
      "skills": {"swordplay": 3, "piloting": 4, "occult": 1},
      "inventory": ["Mach‑IV rapier", "crank‑powered jetpack"],
      "hp": 24,
      "xp": 0,
      "level": 1
  },
  "rules": {  # OSR‑lite default
      "hit_die": 8,
      "proficiency": 2,
      "leveling": {"xp_table": [0, 300, 900, 2700, 6500]}
  },
  "memory": {"k": 6},       # how many memories to retrieve
  "dice": "d20",
  "verbosity": "normal",
  "game_id": random_hash
}

# Save/Load buttons
autoload_checkbox = widgets.Checkbox(value=True, description="Load from Drive")
save_button = widgets.Button(description="Save Config")
load_button = widgets.Button(description="Load Config")
generate_setting_button = widgets.Button(description="Generate Setting")
display(widgets.HBox([autoload_checkbox,save_button, load_button, generate_setting_button]))

CONFIG_PATH = "/content/rpg_config.yaml"
editor = widgets.Textarea(
    value=yaml.dump(default_cfg, sort_keys=False),
    rows=25,
    layout=widgets.Layout(width="100%")
)
display(editor)
def save_cfg_to_file(b=None):
    with open(CONFIG_PATH, "w") as f:
        f.write(editor.value)
    print(f"✅ Config saved to {CONFIG_PATH}")

def load_cfg_from_file(b=None):
    try:
        with open(CONFIG_PATH) as f:
            editor.value = f.read()
        print(f"✅ Config loaded from {CONFIG_PATH}")
    except Exception as e:
        print(f"❌ Error loading config: {e}")
def get_cfg():
  return yaml.safe_load(editor.value)

# ── helper: schema describing the setting object we want back ────────────────
def build_setting_schema():
    """Return a JSON-Schema dict that matches the YAML structure we store."""
    return {
        "type": "object",
        "properties": {
            "setting":  {"type": "string"},
            "tone":     {"type": "string"},
            "intro": {"type": "string"},
            "family_safe": {"type": "boolean"},
            "max_images": {"type": "integer"},
            "pc": {
                "type": "object",
                "properties": {
                    "name": {"type": "string"},
                    "species": {"type": "string"},
                    "skills":  { # Added additionalProperties: false and required: []
                        "type": "object",
                        "properties": {}, # Added properties for clarity, though additionalProperties handles this
                        "required": [], # Added empty required list for skills object
                        "additionalProperties": False
                    },
                    "inventory": {"type": "array", "items": {"type": "string"}},
                    "hp": {"type": "integer"},
                    "xp": {"type": "integer"},
                    "level": {"type": "integer"}
                },
                # Modified required list to include all keys in properties
                "required": ["name", "species", "skills", "inventory", "hp", "xp", "level"],
                "additionalProperties": False
            },
            "rules": { # Added additionalProperties: false and required: []
                "type": "object",
                "properties": {}, # Assuming rules can have properties, add an empty properties object if none are expected
                "required": [], # Added empty required list
                "additionalProperties": False
            },
            "memory": { # Added additionalProperties: false and required: []
                "type": "object",
                "properties": {}, # Assuming memory can have properties, add an empty properties object if none are expected
                "required": [], # Added empty required list
                "additionalProperties": False
            },
            "dice": {"type": "string"},
            "verbosity": {"type": "string"},
            "game_id": {"type": "string"}
        },
        "required": ["setting", "tone", "pc", "rules", "game_id", "family_safe","max_images","memory","dice","verbosity","intro"],
        "additionalProperties": False
    }


def generate_setting_function(b=None):
  """
  Ask the model for a brand-new setting and patch it straight into the YAML
  editor.  Uses STRUCTURED OUTPUTS so the response is guaranteed to match the
  schema above.
  """
  # freshly-seeded randomness for the prompt “garble”
  random.seed(datetime.datetime.now().timestamp())
  varint = random.randint(0, 9_999_999)
  random_hash = hashlib.sha256(os.urandom(16)).hexdigest()

  print(f"Random Bytes: {os.urandom(16).hex()}") # Corrected to generate new random bytes
  print(f"Random SHA256 Hash: {hashlib.sha256(os.urandom(16)).hexdigest()}") # Corrected to generate new random bytes and hash


  prompt = f"""
  You are an imaginative RPG world-builder.
  Generate a concise, ORIGINAL setting paragraph, plus the supplemental data
  outlined below.  Before writing, let the following meaningless noise percolate
  to avoid clichés: {varint} {random_hash}

  Return ONLY valid JSON that matches the given schema.
  """
  # Ask the model, forcing schema compliance  ───────────────────────────────
  schema = build_setting_schema()
  response = client.chat.completions.create(
      model=get_cfg()["model"],      # still reads from YAML
      messages=[{"role": "system", "content": prompt}],
      temperature=1.0,
      max_tokens=350,
      response_format={
          "type": "json_schema",
          "json_schema": {
              "name": "RPGSetting",
              "strict": True,        # requires adherence
              "schema": schema
          }
      }
  )

  # Parse -> merge -> show in editor  ───────────────────────────────────────
  setting_obj = json.loads(response.choices[0].message.content)
  current_cfg = get_cfg()

# Validating LLM Outputs with Pydantic (Hands-On Notebook)

Large language models (LLMs) are amazing at generating text—but not so amazing at consistently following a strict JSON schema.  
That’s where **Pydantic** comes in: it lets you declare what structured data you expect, and then it *enforces* it at runtime.

In this notebook you’ll learn how to:

- Define Pydantic models that describe the shape of your LLM outputs.
- Validate plain JSON from an LLM and get clear errors when something’s wrong.
- Clean and normalize fields (like phone numbers) with custom validators.
- Handle “messy” LLM responses that contain extra text around the JSON.
- Use nested schemas and cross-field validation (e.g., rating vs. average_rating).
- Integrate Pydantic with LLM calls (OpenAI) to safely turn free-form text into typed Python objects.

By the end, you should be able to confidently run LLM calls in a production-ish setting without trusting raw strings.

Code cell 2
-----------
# Install dependencies (uncomment if running in Colab)
!pip install -U "pydantic[email]" openai

Markdown cell 3
---------------
## 1. Why Validate LLM Outputs?

LLMs always produce **text**, even when we ask them for JSON or a very specific format.  
That text can easily contain:

- Misspelled or mismatched field names.
- Wrong data types (e.g., `"5"` as a string vs. `5` as an int).
- Missing required fields or extra unexpected ones.
- Extra commentary or markdown around the “real” JSON.

If you just call `json.loads()` and assume everything is valid:

- You’ll get runtime errors in weird places.
- You won’t know *which* field failed or *why*.
- Debugging becomes painful.

**Pydantic** solves this by:

- Using **type hints** (`str`, `int`, `EmailStr`, etc.) as a runtime contract.
- Automatically converting types where possible.
- Surfacing precise, structured validation errors when something doesn’t match.

We’ll start with a simple example: extracting contact info from an LLM response.

Code cell 4
-----------
from pydantic import BaseModel, EmailStr, field_validator
from typing import Optional


class ContactInfo(BaseModel):
    name: str
    email: EmailStr
    phone: Optional[str] = None
    company: Optional[str] = None

    @field_validator("phone")
    @classmethod
    def validate_phone(cls, v: Optional[str]) -> Optional[str]:
        """Normalize phone numbers and enforce a minimum length."""
        if v is None:
            return v

        cleaned = "".join(ch for ch in v if ch.isdigit())
        if len(cleaned) < 10:
            raise ValueError("Phone number must have at least 10 digits")
        return cleaned

Markdown cell 5
---------------
### Understanding the `ContactInfo` Model

Key ideas illustrated here:

- `ContactInfo(BaseModel)`: every Pydantic model subclasses `BaseModel`.
- Type hints (`name: str`, `email: EmailStr`, etc.) define the schema:
  - `EmailStr` is a special type that validates email format.
  - `Optional[str] = None` means the field can be missing or `null` (`None`).
- `@field_validator("phone")`:
  - Runs **after** parsing to clean and validate a specific field.
  - Here we:
    - Strip everything except digits.
    - Enforce at least 10 digits.
    - Raise `ValueError` if it fails → Pydantic turns this into a clean validation error.

Now let’s pretend this JSON came from an LLM and validate it.

Code cell 6
-----------
import json

# Imagine this came from an LLM call:
llm_response = """
{
    "name": "Sarah Johnson",
    "email": "sarah.johnson@techcorp.com",
    "phone": "(555) 123-4567",
    "company": "TechCorp Industries"
}
"""

data = json.loads(llm_response)
contact = ContactInfo(**data)

print("Name:", contact.name)
print("Email:", contact.email)
print("Phone (normalized):", contact.phone)
print("As dict:", contact.model_dump())

LLMs often return something like:

# Basic OpenAI API Usage

*Updated July 14, 2025*

This notebook teaches the **most up‑to‑date** (July 2025) usage of the OpenAI Python client library (`openai` ≥ 1.x). Each step is preceded by a pedagogical explanation so you can understand *why* we do what we do before running the code.

Markdown cell 2
---------------
## 1  Prerequisites

Before you run any code you will need:

1. **An OpenAI account** with API credit.
2. **Python 3.9+** (check with `python --version`).
3. **The latest OpenAI Python library**  
   Install or upgrade with:

```bash
pip install --upgrade openai
```

4. **An environment variable called `OPENAI_API_KEY`** containing your secret key.

```bash
# macOS / Linux
export OPENAI_API_KEY="sk-...your_key..."

# Windows (PowerShell)
setx OPENAI_API_KEY "sk-...your_key..."
```

Never hard‑code credentials in a notebook – treat them like passwords.

Markdown cell 3
---------------
## 2  Import & authenticate

The OpenAI client automatically reads `OPENAI_API_KEY` from the environment, so a single line constructs a ready‑to‑use `client` object.

Code cell 4
-----------
from openai import OpenAI
from google.colab import userdata

# Get the API key from Colab Secrets
OPENAI_API_KEY = userdata.get('OPENAI_API_KEY')
#if we were in python (no colab) we would use os.env


# Create a client; the key is picked up from the OPENAI_API_KEY env var.
# The API key is automatically picked up from the environment variable
# if set, otherwise you can pass it directly as api_key=OPENAI_API_KEY
client = OpenAI(api_key=OPENAI_API_KEY)


# Quick smoke‑test: list available models (first 5)
for m in client.models.list().data:
    print(m.id)

Markdown cell 5
---------------
## 3  A minimal chat completion

The `chat.completions.create` method takes a list of **messages** following the [Chat ML][] format:

| key | typical values |
|-----|----------------|
| `role` | `"system"`, `"user"`, `"assistant"` |
| `content` | The text of that role |
| `name` (optional) | For tool / function messages |

For a basic single‑turn request we supply a *system* and a *user* message.

[Chat ML]: https://platform.openai.com/docs/guides/text-generation/chat-completions

Code cell 6
-----------
response = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="gpt-4.1-nano",  # Ultra‑fast model (July 2025)
    messages=[
        {"role": "system", "content": "You are a concise assistant."},
        {"role": "user", "content": "Explain transformers in one sentence."}
    ]
)
response.choices[0].message.content

---------------
## 4  Streaming tokens as they arrive (optional)

Setting `stream=True` yields an iterator of *chunks* so you can print tokens in real time, perfect for chat UIs.

Code cell 8

stream = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="gpt-4o-mini",
    messages=[
        {"role": "user", "content": "Write a haiku about Michigan summers."}
    ],
    stream=True
)
import time
partial = ""
for chunk in stream:
    delta = chunk.choices[0].delta.content
    partial += delta or ""
    print(delta or "", end="", flush=True)
    time.sleep(0.1)

print("\n\n---\nFull response length:", len(partial))

# Module 3 – Getting Started with the OpenAI Responses API

In this notebook, we'll:

- Install and configure the latest OpenAI Python client.
- Initialize the `OpenAI` client.
- Call the **Responses API** for simple text generation.
- Use **system** vs **user** roles to shape behavior (chat-style usage).
- Control model behavior with parameters like `temperature` and `max_output_tokens`.

This will be our "Hello, LLM" notebook that we use in class to show how to connect Python code to a hosted large language model.

Code cell 2
-----------
# If you're in Colab or a fresh environment, run this once:
!pip install --upgrade openai

Markdown cell 3
---------------
## 1. Import and initialize the OpenAI client

The new OpenAI Python library (v1.x) uses an `OpenAI` client object.

We will:

1. Import `OpenAI` from the `openai` package.
2. Create a client instance.
3. Assume your API key is stored in the `OPENAI_API_KEY` environment variable.

If you're in Colab, you can set the environment variable with:
- `os.environ["OPENAI_API_KEY"] = "sk-..."` (NOT recommended to commit to Git),
- or use Colab's secret storage / environment variable UI.

Code cell 4
-----------
from openai import OpenAI
from google.colab import userdata
import os
# Get the API key from Colab Secrets
OPENAI_API_KEY = userdata.get('OPENAI_API_KEY')

# Create a client; the key is picked up from the OPENAI_API_KEY env var.
# The API key is automatically picked up from the environment variable
# if set, otherwise you can pass it directly as api_key=OPENAI_API_KEY
client = OpenAI(api_key=OPENAI_API_KEY)


# Quick smoke‑test: list available models (first 5)
for m in client.models.list().data:
    print(m.id)

print("Client initialized:", type(client))

Markdown cell 5
---------------
## 2. The Responses API: one API, many use cases

The **Responses API** is the newer, unified endpoint that can:

- Generate text (like the old Completions / Chat Completions APIs).
- Call tools, browse the web, and orchestrate simple agent-like workflows (later in the course).
- Return different output "modalities" (text, images, etc.) from the same endpoint.  

Today we will just:

- Send **text input**.
- Get a **text output**.
- Optionally use simple "roles" (`system`, `user`) to shape how the model responds.

Code cell 6
-----------
# 3.1 Simple: single-string input

response = client.responses.create(
    model="gpt-4.1-mini",  # Or another text-capable model from the docs
    input="Write a short, friendly welcome message to students starting a Generative AI class.",
    max_output_tokens=150,
    temperature=0.7,
)

# The Responses API returns a structured object.
# We’ll inspect it to understand the structure.
print(response)

Markdown cell 7
---------------
## 3. Extracting the generated text

The response object contains a list of "output" items.  
Each output item has a list of "content" blocks (e.g., text blocks).

We'll grab the first output, then the first content block, and read its `.text` field.

(If the structure ever changes, you can always `print(response)` again and inspect the JSON-like output.)

Code cell 8
-----------
def get_text_from_response(resp):
    """
    Helper to safely extract text from a Responses API call.
    This assumes the response contains at least one text block.
    """
    try:
        first_output = resp.output[0]
        first_block = first_output.content[0]

        # In the current API, text is stored on a `.text` field.
        # Some versions may wrap it further; adjust if needed.
        text_value = getattr(first_block, "text", None)

        # If it's an object with `.value`, extract that.
        if hasattr(text_value, "value"):
            return text_value.value

        # Otherwise assume it's already a string.
        return str(text_value)
    except Exception as e:
        return f"[Could not extract text cleanly: {e}]"

print(get_text_from_response(response))

# 🦙 Lesson 2 — Inside the LLaMA Family
We’ll explore Meta’s LLaMA lineage, motivation, design choices, and how they differ from early GPT‑style models.

Markdown cell 2

## 📚 Motivation behind LLaMA
- **Research accessibility**: Provide state‑of‑the‑art weights to researchers under a non‑commercial license.
- **Efficient scaling**: Utilize smaller vocab, Rotary Embeddings, and grouped‑query attention in v2/3.
- **Instruction‑fine‑tuning**: LLaMA‑3‑Instruct rivals GPT‑3.5 quality with fewer parameters.

Markdown cell 3

## 🔍 Architectural Highlights vs. GPT‑2/3

Markdown cell 4
---------------

import torch
from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoTokenizer

model_id = "meta-llama/Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct"

# Load tokenizer & model
tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(model_id)
model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(
    model_id,
    device_map="auto",
    torch_dtype="auto",
  # bitsandbytes 4-bit loading
)

def generate_text(
    prompt: str,
    max_new_tokens: int = 128,
    temperature: float = 0.7,
    top_p: float = 0.9,
    do_sample: bool = True,
):
    # Tokenize & move to the model's device
    inputs = tokenizer(prompt, return_tensors="pt").to(model.device)

    # Some models don't define pad_token; fall back to eos
    pad_id = tokenizer.pad_token_id if tokenizer.pad_token_id is not None else tokenizer.eos_token_id

    with torch.no_grad():
        output_ids = model.generate(
            **inputs,
            max_new_tokens=max_new_tokens,
            temperature=temperature,
            top_p=top_p,
            do_sample=do_sample,
            eos_token_id=tokenizer.eos_token_id,
            pad_token_id=pad_id,
        )

    # Decode the full sequence (prompt + generation)
    full_text = tokenizer.decode(output_ids[0], skip_special_tokens=True)

    # If you only want *new* tokens beyond the prompt:
    gen_only_ids = output_ids[0, inputs["input_ids"].shape[1]:]
    gen_text = tokenizer.decode(gen_only_ids, skip_special_tokens=True)

    return full_text, gen_text

full, only_new = generate_text("Tell me a haiku about transformers and attention:")
print("=== Full Text ===")
print(full)
print("\n=== Generated Continuation ===")
print(only_new.strip())

# 🏠 Lesson 4 (Extended) — Local Deployment *and* OpenAI‑Compatible APIs Across Providers

**Goal:** Give you & your students a *working mental model + runnable code scaffolds* for serving and calling **small & mid‑sized open‑source language models (SLMs)** locally *and* via hosted services — all through a mostly **OpenAI‑style client interface** so you can swap backends with minimal code changes.

We’ll cover:

1. **Why run locally?** Privacy, latency, offline, cost ceilings.
2. **Hardware & quantization cheat sheet** for LLaMA / Qwen / Gemma.
3. **Local inference libraries:** `llama-cpp-python`, `vLLM`, Hugging Face **Text Generation Inference (TGI)**.
4. **Launching OpenAI‑compatible servers** (local + cloud).
5. **Querying ANY of them using the official `openai` Python library** by pointing `base_url=...`.
6. **Routing + multi‑vendor abstraction** with **LiteLLM**.
7. **API key management in Colab** (env vars, secrets).
8. **Usage & cost monitoring** (OpenAI Usage & Cost APIs; DIY dashboards).
9. **Putting it together:** Hybrid pipeline that chooses *local SLM* first, falls back to *cloud LLM* when needed.

Let's get set up. 👇

        f"User: {user_input}\n"

        max_tokens=200,  # Adjust as needed

        top_p=0.9,  # Nucleus sampling
        repeat_penalty=1.1,  # Penalize repetitive phrases
        stop=["User:", "AI:"],
        n_ctx = 1024
    )
   # Extract the text response
    ai_response = response["choices"][0]["text"].strip()

# 🦙 llama‑cpp‑python Colab Demo (2025)

This Colab shows how to **download an FP16 GGUF model, quantize it, and run inference** using the latest [`llama‑cpp‑python`](https://github.com/abetlen/llama-cpp-python) bindings citeturn11search2.

**Contents**  
1. Installation (GPU or CPU)  
2. Download an FP16 GGUF checkpoint from 🤗 Hub  
3. Quantize to Q4\_K\_M (4‑bit) with `llama_cpp.quantize`  
4. Load with `Llama()` and generate text  
5. Bonus: Chat‐style helper & embeddings  

> **Tip** Adjust paths, model names, and `ftype` constants to match the model/quant format you want.

Markdown cell 2
---------------
## 1  Installation
Choose **one** of the two cells below depending on whether you want GPU acceleration.

Code cell 3
-----------
# 🚀 GPU build (cuBLAS). Takes 2–4 min on Colab.
# Comment this cell out if you only want CPU.
%env CMAKE_ARGS=-DLLAMA_CUBLAS=on
%env FORCE_CMAKE=1
!pip install -U --quiet llama-cpp-python==0.3.7 huggingface_hub

Code cell 4
-----------
# 🖥️ CPU‑only build (fast install, smaller wheel)
# Uncomment if you skipped the GPU cell above.
# !pip install -U --quiet llama-cpp-python==0.3.7 huggingface_hub

Markdown cell 5
---------------
## 2  Download an FP16 GGUF model

Code cell 6
-----------
from huggingface_hub import hf_hub_download

REPO_ID = "TheBloke/Qwen1.5-1.8B-Base-GGUF"   # ↩️ change to any GGUF repo
F16_FILE = "qwen1_5-1_8b-base.F16.gguf"       # ↩️ exact filename

model_f16_path = hf_hub_download(repo_id=REPO_ID, filename=F16_FILE, local_dir="models")
print("Downloaded:", model_f16_path)

Markdown cell 7
---------------
## 3  Quantize to `Q4_K_M`
This step converts the ~2.4 GB **FP16** file to a ~800 MB 4‑bit file.

Code cell 8
-----------
from llama_cpp import quantize, llama_cpp
import os, pathlib, time

out_path = pathlib.Path("models") / F16_FILE.replace("F16", "Q4_K_M")

# `ftype` constants live under llama_cpp and correspond
# to names like LLAMA_FTYPE_MOSTLY_Q4_K_M in the C API.
ftype = llama_cpp.LLAMA_FTYPE_MOSTLY_Q4_K_M   # 4‑bit groupwise mixed

t0 = time.time()
quantize(
    model_f16_path,
    str(out_path),
    n_threads=os.cpu_count() or 8,
    ftype=ftype,
)
print(f"Quantized model saved to: {out_path}  (took {time.time()-t0:.1f}s)")

# 🧠 Lesson 1 — LLMs vs. SLMs
Welcome! In this section we’ll clarify **Large Language Models (LLMs)** and **Small Language Models (SLMs)**, explain why model size matters, and explore the trade‑offs you encounter when choosing a model size for real projects.

Markdown cell 3
---------------
## 🔧 Colab Setup
Run the cell below to install everything used across *all* notebooks in this series. Skip if you’ve already executed it in a previous notebook session.

Code cell 4
-----------
!pip -q install --upgrade transformers accelerate bitsandbytes datasets huggingface_hub
!pip -q install --upgrade sentencepiece einops rich

Markdown cell 5
---------------
## 📘 Key Definitions

Markdown cell 6
---------------
**LLM (Large Language Model)**  
- Typically ≥ 13 B parameters (B = **Billion**).  
- Optimized for broad coverage, multilingual skills, chain‑of‑thought, etc.  
- Heavy compute & memory footprint.

**SLM (Small Language Model)**  
- Anywhere from 100 M to ~13 B parameters.  
- Faster, cheaper, often easier to fine‑tune locally.  
- May specialize (e.g., Qwen‑1.5‑0.5B excels at code‑completion in resource‑constrained settings).

### Where SLMs Excel
1. **Edge & Mobile inference**  
2. **On‑prem or air‑gapped deployments**  
3. **Low‑latency voice assistants**  
4. **Rapid experimentation / prototyping**

Markdown cell 7
---------------
## 📏 Param Count vs. Capability
Below we’ll grab configs for three models of different sizes and compare their parameter counts.

Code cell 8
-----------
from transformers import AutoConfig
models = ['meta-llama/Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct',
          'google/gemma-2b-it',
          'meta-llama/Meta-Llama-3-8B-Instruct']
for m in models:
    cfg = AutoConfig.from_pretrained(m)
    # Calculate the number of parameters manually based on the config
    if hasattr(cfg, 'num_parameters'):
      num_params = cfg.num_parameters()
    elif hasattr(cfg, 'n_params'):
      num_params = cfg.n_params
    elif hasattr(cfg, 'num_attention_heads') and hasattr(cfg, 'hidden_size') and hasattr(cfg, 'intermediate_size') and hasattr(cfg, 'vocab_size'):
        # This is a simplified calculation and might not be perfectly accurate for all models
        num_params = 2 * cfg.num_hidden_layers * cfg.hidden_size * cfg.intermediate_size + cfg.vocab_size * cfg.hidden_size
    else:
        num_params = 'N/A' # Cannot calculate parameters with available attributes

    print(f'{m:<55} → {cfg.num_hidden_layers:>2} layers, {cfg.hidden_size:>4} dim, ~{num_params:,} parameters')

# Memory Math & LoRA Calculator 📊
**Objective:** Enter *any* Hugging Face model ID (or manual parameter count) and instantly see:
1.  FP32 / FP16 / BF16 / INT8 / INT4 memory footprints.
2.  Extra parameters & memory for a LoRA adapter (configurable *r* and target modules).

Designed for quick What‑If experiments during class.

Code cell 2
-----------
## 📦 Install & Imports
!pip -q install transformers peft accelerate -U
import torch, pandas as pd, math, gc
from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoConfig
from peft import LoraConfig, get_peft_model, TaskType

Markdown cell 3
---------------
## 1️⃣ Provide Base Model

Code cell 4
-----------
def get_param_count(model_id=None, manual_m=None):
    """Return parameter count (int) for a HF model or manual value in millions."""
    if manual_m is not None:
        return int(manual_m * 1e6)
    cfg = AutoConfig.from_pretrained(model_id)
    # Calculate parameters based on common attributes like hidden_size and num_hidden_layers
    # This is a simplified approach and might not be accurate for all models
    if hasattr(cfg, 'num_parameters'):
        print('Using num_parameters from config')
        return cfg.num_parameters
    elif hasattr(cfg, 'hidden_size') and hasattr(cfg, 'num_hidden_layers'):
        print('Using hidden_size and num_hidden_layers from config')
        # This is a rough estimation and might not be precise for all architectures
        # A more accurate way would be to load the model and count parameters
        return cfg.hidden_size * cfg.hidden_size * cfg.num_hidden_layers * 12 # simplified calculation
    else:
        raise AttributeError(f"Could not determine parameter count for model {model_id}")


# 👉 Edit here:
BASE_MODEL_ID = 'facebook/opt-125m'  # or None
MANUAL_PARAM_M = None  # e.g., 7000 for 7B

PARAMS = get_param_count(BASE_MODEL_ID, MANUAL_PARAM_M)
print(f'Base params: {PARAMS/1e6:.1f} M for model {BASE_MODEL_ID}')

Markdown cell 5
---------------
## 2️⃣ Memory Footprint Table

Code cell 6
-----------
def memory_table(params: int):
    bytes_fp32 = params * 4
    dtype_bytes = {'FP32':4, 'FP16':2, 'BF16':2, 'INT8':1, 'INT4':0.5}
    rows = []
    for dtype, b in dtype_bytes.items():
        rows.append({'dtype': dtype, 'Memory_GB': round(bytes_fp32 * (b/4) / 1e9, 2)})
    return pd.DataFrame(rows)

mem_df = memory_table(PARAMS)
mem_df

Markdown cell 7
---------------
## 3️⃣ LoRA Adapter → Param & Memory

Code cell 8
-----------
def lora_stats(model_id, r=8, alpha=16, target_modules=('q_proj', 'v_proj')):
    base_model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(model_id, torch_dtype=torch.float16 if torch.cuda.is_available() else torch.float32)
    lora_cfg = LoraConfig(r=r, lora_alpha=alpha, target_modules=list(target_modules), bias='none', task_type=TaskType.CAUSAL_LM)
    lora_model = get_peft_model(base_model, lora_cfg)
    base_params = sum(p.numel() for p in base_model.parameters())
    lora_total = sum(p.numel() for p in lora_model.parameters())
    lora_only = lora_total - base_params
    del base_model, lora_model
    gc.collect()
    return base_params, lora_only

# 👉 Edit r / alpha as desired
BASE, LORA_ONLY = lora_stats(BASE_MODEL_ID, r=8, alpha=16)
print(f'LoRA added params: {LORA_ONLY/1e6:.2f} M  ({LORA_ONLY/BASE:.2%} of base)')
print(f'Approx adapter memory FP16: {LORA_ONLY*2/1e9:.2f} GB')

# Quick‑Fix Grab Bag 🛠️
**Purpose:** Rapid, copy‑pastable solutions for three common hiccups that derail early‑stage fine‑tuning sessions:
1. Token‑length explosions
2. GPU Out‑Of‑Memory (OOM) errors
3. Faulty train/validation splits

Run each section independently or top‑to‑bottom. Designed for a Colab T4/CPU runtime.

Code cell 2
-----------
## 📦 Install / Imports
# (Collapse this cell after running)
!pip -q install transformers datasets torch accelerate -U
import torch, random, json, os, gc, textwrap
from datasets import load_dataset, Dataset
from transformers import AutoTokenizer

Markdown cell 3
---------------
## 1️⃣ Token‑Length Pruning Helper

Code cell 4
-----------
def prune_to_context(texts, tokenizer, max_tokens=2048):
    """Truncate each string in *texts* to *max_tokens* using the provided tokenizer."""
    pruned = []
    for t in texts:
        tokens = tokenizer(t, truncation=True, max_length=max_tokens, add_special_tokens=False)
        pruned.append(tokenizer.decode(tokens['input_ids']))
    return pruned

# 🔍 Demo
tok = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained('facebook/opt-125m')
demo_text = ["Lorem ipsum " * 500]
print(len(tok(demo_text[0])['input_ids']), 'tokens before')
short = prune_to_context(demo_text, tok, 128)
print(len(tok(short[0])['input_ids']), 'tokens after')

Markdown cell 5
---------------
## 2️⃣ GPU Out‑Of‑Memory Patch

Code cell 6
-----------
def try_forward(model, **kwargs):
    """Safe forward pass that frees cache on CUDA OOM and retries on CPU."""
    try:
        return model(**kwargs)
    except RuntimeError as e:
        if 'out of memory' in str(e).lower():
            print('⚠️ CUDA OOM – retrying on CPU…')
            torch.cuda.empty_cache()
            gc.collect()
            model_cpu = model.to('cpu')
            return model_cpu(**kwargs)
        raise

# Usage example (pseudo‑code):
# output = try_forward(my_model, input_ids=batch['input_ids'])

Markdown cell 7
---------------
## 3️⃣ Train/Validation Split Sanity Checker

Code cell 8
-----------
def check_split_overlap(ds_train: Dataset, ds_val: Dataset, key='text'):
    """Print overlap percentage between two datasets on a text column."""
    set_train = set(ds_train[key])
    set_val   = set(ds_val[key])
    overlap = len(set_train & set_val)
    total = min(len(set_train), len(set_val))
    print(f'🔎 Overlap: {overlap} records ({overlap/total:.2%})')

# Quick demo using a tiny dummy dataset
dummy = Dataset.from_dict({'text': [f'sample {i}' for i in range(10)]})
split = dummy.train_test_split(test_size=0.3, seed=42)
check_split_overlap(split['train'], split['test'])

Try each exercise first, then open the hints only when you are stuck. ## Learning outcomes By the end, you should be able to: - Install and verify a modern Hugging Face environment. - Use task pipelines for quick inference. - Choose checkpoints from the Hugging Face Hub based on task and model card information. - Load tokenizers, processors, configs, and task-specific models with `Auto*` classes. - Tokenize text, batch inputs, pad, truncate, decode, and inspect attention masks. - Run manual PyTorch inference for classification, embeddings, and generation. - Use chat templates for chat/instruction models when supported. - Understand image, audio, and multimodal preprocessing patterns. - Prepare datasets for training. - Fine-tune a classifier with `Trainer`. - Save, reload, and optionally share models. - Debug common beginner errors systematically. ## Recommended runtime Most early sections run on CPU. Fine-tuning and generation sections are much more pleasant on a GPU runtime such as Google Colab T4. ## Notebook rule Every exercise has an empty code cell. Do not paste the hint immediately. Try first. The hint is the safety net. ## 0. Concept map: the Transformers workflow A typical Transformers workflow is: ```text Hugging Face Hub checkpoint id ↓ from_pretrained(...) ↓ tokenizer / image processor / feature extractor / processor ↓ model config + model weights ↓ pipeline() OR manual inference OR Trainer fine-tuning ↓ save_pretrained(...) / push_to_hub(...) ``` The most common beginner objects are: | Object | Examples | Purpose | |---|---|---| | High-level inference | `pipeline()` | Simple task API for inference | | Text preprocessing | `AutoTokenizer` | Text to token IDs and tensors | | Vision preprocessing | `AutoImageProcessor` | Images to pixel tensors | | Audio preprocessing | `AutoFeatureExtractor`, `AutoProcessor` | Audio to features/tensors | | Multimodal preprocessing | `AutoProcessor` | Bundles text/image/audio preprocessing | | Config | `AutoConfig` | Metadata about architecture, labels, and task | | Base model | `AutoModel` | Hidden states / embeddings | | Task model | `AutoModelForSequenceClassification`, `AutoModelForCausalLM`, etc. | Model plus task head | | Batch builder | `DataCollatorWithPadding`, task collators | Pads/forms training batches | | Trainer API | `TrainingArguments`, `Trainer` | Standard PyTorch training loop abstraction | | Save/load | `save_pretrained()`, `from_pretrained()` | Reuse local or Hub artifacts | ### 0.1 Install the Hugging Face stack Install the libraries used throughout this notebook. `transformers` provides the models and pipelines, `datasets` loads and processes datasets, `evaluate` provides metrics, `accelerate` supports training/device workflows, and `safetensors` is the safer tensor serialization format. **Your task** 1. Install or upgrade `transformers`, `datasets`, `evaluate`, `accelerate`, `safetensors`, `sentencepiece`, `torch`, `pillow`, and `requests`. 2. Restart the runtime/kernel after installation if your environment asks you to. **Expected checkpoint:** The install should finish without errors. Restart the runtime if prompted.
Hint 1 — click only after you try ```python !pip install -U transformers datasets evaluate accelerate safetensors sentencepiece torch pillow requests ```
```python ``` ### 0.2 Verify versions and hardware Environment mismatches are a major source of ML frustration. Always check versions and hardware before debugging model code. **Your task** 1. Import `transformers`, `datasets`, `evaluate`, and `torch`. 2. Print each package version. 3. Print whether CUDA is available. 4. Create a variable named `device` equal to `'cuda'` if available, otherwise `'cpu'`. **Expected checkpoint:** You should see package versions and a device value.
Hint 1 — click only after you try ```python import transformers, datasets, evaluate, torch print("transformers:", transformers.__version__) print("datasets:", datasets.__version__) print("evaluate:", evaluate.__version__) print("torch:", torch.__version__) print("CUDA available:", torch.cuda.is_available()) device = "cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu" print("device:", device) ```
```python ``` ### 0.3 Create a reusable inspection helper Transformers objects contain useful metadata. A tiny helper function makes it easier to inspect configs and models throughout the notebook. **Your task** 1. Define `show_model_summary(obj)`. 2. It should print the Python class name. 3. If the object has a `.config`, inspect that; otherwise inspect the object itself. 4. Print common fields when present: `model_type`, `architectures`, `num_labels`, `id2label`, `vocab_size`, `hidden_size`, `num_hidden_layers`, and `num_attention_heads`. **Expected checkpoint:** The helper should define without errors.
Hint 1 — click only after you try ```python def show_model_summary(obj): print("Python class:", obj.__class__.__name__) cfg = getattr(obj, "config", obj) for attr in [ "model_type", "architectures", "num_labels", "id2label", "vocab_size", "hidden_size", "num_hidden_layers", "num_attention_heads" ]: if hasattr(cfg, attr): print(f"{attr}:", getattr(cfg, attr)) ```
```python ``` --- # Part 1 — High-level inference with `pipeline()` `pipeline()` is the easiest entry point. It wraps preprocessing, model inference, and postprocessing behind a task-oriented API. Common pipeline tasks include: - `sentiment-analysis` / `text-classification` - `zero-shot-classification` - `token-classification` - `question-answering` - `fill-mask` - `summarization` - `translation` - `text-generation` - `feature-extraction` - `image-classification` - `automatic-speech-recognition` Important beginner rule: **the pipeline task, model checkpoint, and expected input format must match.** ### 1.1 First pipeline: sentiment analysis A sentiment pipeline takes text and returns a label and score. This is the fastest way to confirm your environment can download and run a pretrained model. **Your task** 1. Import `pipeline` from `transformers`. 2. Create a `sentiment-analysis` pipeline. 3. Pass it three sentences: positive, negative, and ambiguous. 4. Print the raw output. **Expected checkpoint:** You should see a list of dictionaries containing labels and scores.
Hint 1 — click only after you try ```python from transformers import pipeline sentiment_pipe = pipeline("sentiment-analysis") texts = [ "This notebook is clear and helpful.", "Dependency errors make me want to flip the table.", "The model ran quickly, but the output was surprising." ] sentiment_pipe(texts) ```
```python ``` ### 1.2 Inspect the pipeline internals A pipeline object usually contains a task name, model, tokenizer or processor, and device information. Inspecting these demystifies the abstraction. **Your task** 1. Print the pipeline task. 2. Print the model class. 3. Print the tokenizer class if present. 4. Use `show_model_summary()` on the pipeline model. **Expected checkpoint:** You should see which model and tokenizer were loaded.
Hint 1 — click only after you try ```python print("Task:", sentiment_pipe.task) print("Model class:", sentiment_pipe.model.__class__.__name__) print("Tokenizer class:", sentiment_pipe.tokenizer.__class__.__name__) show_model_summary(sentiment_pipe.model) ```
```python ``` ### 1.3 Use an explicit checkpoint When you do not specify a model, the library may choose a default. In real projects, choose checkpoints intentionally based on model cards, task fit, license, and size. **Your task** 1. Create a second sentiment pipeline with the explicit model id `distilbert/distilbert-base-uncased-finetuned-sst-2-english`. 2. Run the same texts. 3. Compare outputs. **Expected checkpoint:** The results should be similar, but now the checkpoint is explicit.
Hint 1 — click only after you try ```python explicit_sentiment = pipeline( "sentiment-analysis", model="distilbert/distilbert-base-uncased-finetuned-sst-2-english" ) explicit_sentiment(texts) ```
```python ``` ### 1.4 Zero-shot classification Zero-shot classification lets you provide labels at inference time. It is useful for quick prototypes when you do not have a task-specific fine-tuned classifier. **Your task** 1. Create a `zero-shot-classification` pipeline using `facebook/bart-large-mnli`. 2. Classify a paragraph about learning Transformers. 3. Use candidate labels: `education`, `technology`, `sports`, `politics`, and `entertainment`. 4. Inspect the ranked labels and scores. **Expected checkpoint:** The top labels should likely include education and/or technology.
Hint 1 — click only after you try ```python zero_shot = pipeline("zero-shot-classification", model="facebook/bart-large-mnli") sequence = "Students are learning how tokenizers, pretrained models, and fine-tuning workflows fit together." labels = ["education", "technology", "sports", "politics", "entertainment"] zero_shot(sequence, candidate_labels=labels) ```
```python ``` ### 1.5 Token classification / NER Token classification predicts labels for tokens or spans. Named Entity Recognition is the classic example. **Your task** 1. Create a `token-classification` pipeline. 2. Use `aggregation_strategy='simple'`. 3. Run it on a sentence containing a person, organization, and location. 4. Print entity group, word, score, and span. **Expected checkpoint:** You should see extracted entity-like spans, though small/default models are not perfect.
Hint 1 — click only after you try ```python ner = pipeline("token-classification", aggregation_strategy="simple") text = "Charles teaches AI classes for Global Information Technology in Michigan." for ent in ner(text): print(ent["entity_group"], ent["word"], round(ent["score"], 3), ent["start"], ent["end"]) ```
```python ``` ### 1.6 Extractive question answering Extractive QA predicts an answer span from a provided context. It does not answer from general memory; the answer must be in the context. **Your task** 1. Create a `question-answering` pipeline. 2. Write a short context paragraph about Transformers. 3. Ask two questions with answers directly in the context. 4. Print answers and scores. **Expected checkpoint:** Answers should be spans from the context.
Hint 1 — click only after you try ```python qa = pipeline("question-answering") context = """ Transformers provides pretrained models for text, vision, audio, and multimodal tasks. Pipelines are useful for quick inference. Auto classes give more control over tokenizers, processors, configurations, and model heads. """ for question in ["What are pipelines useful for?", "What do Auto classes give more control over?"]: print(question) print(qa(question=question, context=context)) ```

# Fine-Tuning a 3B-Parameter Language Model: Comprehensive Plan & Design
## 1. Overview and Goals
This document outlines a complete training regimen for fine-tuning a ~3B parameter language model on various possible tasks, with minimal hardware (e.g. a single consumer GPU). The plan is modular and covers decision points for different scenarios (decoder-only vs. encoder-decoder models, supervised vs. RL fine-tuning, etc.). We target efficient methods like Hugging Face (HF) Transformers, PEFT (LoRA), accelerate/DeepSpeed for scaling, and quantization (via BitsAndBytes 8-bit/4-bit, GPTQ, GGUF) to enable training and inference on limited hardware. Each section details options with pros/cons, accuracy vs. resource trade-offs, and code examples to guide implementation.
Scope of Tasks: The fine-tuning workflow should accommodate: - Standard NLP tasks or instruction following (e.g. QA, reasoning, domain-specific text). - Personalized data fine-tuning (e.g. on a user’s own writings). - Interactive or control tasks (e.g. an LLM controlling a video game or agent via text actions).
We assume the base model is decoder-only (e.g. GPT-style) for concreteness, but we note how to adapt for encoder-decoder or multi-modal models at decision points. The plan emphasizes efficient fine-tuning (possibly on a single GPU with <24 GB memory) by using parameter-efficient methods and quantization, without sacrificing much performance. We also cover multiple fine-tuning techniques: from Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) to Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) and newer RL variants (like PPO, DPO, GRPO, etc.), highlighting their trade-offs.
## 2. Model Selection and Architecture Considerations
Base Model Choice: Start with a pre-trained language model of ~3B parameters. Examples include EleutherAI/gpt-neo-2.7B, facebook/opt-2.7b or a LLaMA2 3B variant. A decoder-only model is assumed (suitable for generative tasks and RL policies). Key considerations:
- Decoder-Only vs. Encoder-Decoder: If using an encoder-decoder (e.g. T5, BART), the fine-tuning workflow changes slightly (you would fine-tune both encoder and decoder on paired input-output data, and some PEFT methods like LoRA apply differently to encoder/decoder components). Decoder-only models are simpler for generation tasks, so we focus on those, but the outlined methods (LoRA, QLoRA, quantization) are largely applicable to encoder-decoders as well.
- Modalities: This plan primarily covers text-based models. If modalities like vision or audio are involved (e.g. a vision-language model for game state images), additional steps would be needed (like using a vision encoder or multi-modal model). The quantization and PEFT techniques we discuss support other modalities in many cases (bitsandbytes can quantize any linear layers, even in ViTs or Whisper models). However, multi-modal fine-tuning might require task-specific data pipelines beyond this document’s scope.
Memory Footprint Estimates: A 3B model in full 32-bit floats requires ~12 GB GPU RAM just to load (approximately 4 GB per billion parameters). In 16-bit (FP16/BF16) it’s ~2 GB per billion (~6 GB for 3B). We will leverage lower precision to fit the model and optimizer states in a single GPU memory: for instance, 8-bit model weights can cut memory by 4× vs FP32. For much larger models, 4-bit quantization can be used to fit models up to 30B+ on a 24 GB GPU, but for a ~3B model 8-bit or 16-bit precision will suffice on most consumer GPUs.
Plan Outline: We will next cover data preparation, then two main training routes:
Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) – fine-tuning on a static dataset of prompts and correct outputs.
Reinforcement Learning Fine-Tuning (RL-based) – tuning with a reward signal (e.g. human feedback or game score), including RLHF, PPO/GRPO, etc.
For each, we will compare full-model fine-tuning vs. parameter-efficient tuning, and how to optimize memory and compute. Finally, we discuss model quantization and inference deployment (HF pipelines vs. llama-cpp for CPU).
## 3. Dataset Preparation and Preprocessing
Identify or Construct the Dataset: The fine-tuning task and data format can vary: - Instruction/QA/Chat Fine-Tuning: Data may be a list of prompts and desired responses (e.g. instruction ➔ solution). For example, a JSON or CSV of {"prompt": ..., "response": ...} pairs. If the task is reasoning, the responses might include detailed step-by-step answers (chain-of-thought). If domain-specific, the data might be documents with known outputs or demonstrations. - Preference Data (for RLHF/DPO): Pairs of model outputs ranked by preference, or a dataset of queries with multiple answers and human feedback. This is needed if doing RLHF (to train a reward model or directly for DPO). - Behavior Cloning for Control: If the task is game control, you might have a dataset of state-action sequences (e.g. text descriptions of game state and the action taken). If not, you may start with an SFT on simulated interactions or use RL from scratch with an environment.
Loading and Preprocessing: Use Hugging Face Datasets to load and preprocess data efficiently. For example:
```python
from datasets import load_dataset

# Example: loading a JSONL with prompt-response pairs
data = load_dataset('json', data_files='finetune_data.jsonl')
train_data = data['train']

# Preprocessing: concatenate prompt and response into model input format
def format_example(example):
    prompt = example['prompt']
    answer = example['response']
    example['input_text'] = f"{prompt}\n### Response:\n{answer}"
    return example

train_data = train_data.map(format_example)
print(train_data[0]['input_text'][:200])
```
This snippet shows how to load a dataset and format each entry as a single text for a causal LM (including a separator like “### Response:” to delineate prompt vs. answer). The exact formatting depends on how the model was pre-trained (for instance, LLaMA-based models often use <s> or system/user tokens in a chat format). Consistency in formatting is important to get good results.
Data Cleaning: Ensure the data is clean and relevant. Remove any sensitive personal information if fine-tuning on personal data. Filter out extremely long sequences if they exceed the model’s context length (for a 3B model, context might be 1024 or 2048 tokens). For reasoning tasks, verify that ground-truth reasoning steps are correct. If doing RLHF, make sure preference labels are consistent and reliable (or use AI-generated feedback if human labels are scarce, acknowledging the risk of bias).
Train/Val Split: Reserve a portion of data for validation. This helps monitor overfitting and choose the best model. With limited data (like personal data), you might use cross-validation or evaluate on qualitatively held-out prompts.
Batching and Tokenization: Use a Tokenizer from HF Transformers with the model’s vocab. Pre-tokenize the data and possibly truncate or chunk if needed. If doing causal LM fine-tuning, typically concatenate prompt and response as a single input sequence. We may need to create an appropriate data collator that:
Pads sequences to the same length per batch.
For causal LM, can set labels = input_ids (masking out prompt tokens’ loss if needed, in instruction tuning tasks where we only want to predict the response part).
Example using a data collator for causal language modeling:
```python
from transformers import AutoTokenizer, DataCollatorForLanguageModeling

tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(base_model_name)
collator = DataCollatorForLanguageModeling(tokenizer, mlm=False)  # for causal LM

def tokenize_batch(batch):
    return tokenizer(batch['input_text'], truncation=True, padding='max_length', 
                     max_length=1024)  # or use dynamic padding in collator

tokenized_data = train_data.map(tokenize_batch, batched=True, remove_columns=train_data.column_names)
```
(This prepares tokenized input IDs with padding. We set mlm=False because we’re doing auto-regressive LM fine-tuning, not masked LM.)
Special Case – RL Datasets: If planning RLHF, you often need: - A supervised dataset for initial fine-tuning (Step 1 of RLHF). - A preference dataset for reward model training (pairs of outputs ranked). - For pure RL on a game: possibly an environment simulator instead of a fixed dataset. In that case, data preparation involves writing an environment loop rather than a static dataset (discussed in RL section).
In summary, data prep results in train_dataset (and eval_dataset) ready for the training loop. With data ready, we move to choosing a fine-tuning strategy.
## 4. Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) Strategies
In supervised fine-tuning, we train the model to mimic the desired outputs in the dataset. There are multiple approaches:
### 4.1 Full Model Fine-Tuning (Update All Weights)
Description: All model parameters are updated via gradient descent on the task data. This requires the most memory and compute, but maximizes flexibility (the model can fully adjust to new data).
Pros: - Potentially highest task performance since every weight can adapt. - Simpler implementation: just load the model and train with an optimizer over all params.
Cons: - Memory/Compute Intensive: A 3B model has 3B * 2 bytes (FP16) ≈ 6 GB of weights, plus optimizer states (another ~6 GB if using Adam). On a single GPU with limited memory, this might not fit comfortably with reasonable batch sizes. Gradient accumulation or multi-GPU might be needed. - Higher risk of overfitting on small datasets (since so many parameters can adjust). - Not feasible for larger models on one GPU (thus not scalable beyond a certain size without distributed training).
When to use: If the model is small enough and the dataset is large/important enough to warrant full re-training. On a 3B model with a 12–24 GB GPU, full fine-tuning is possible in FP16 with small batches, but if you push beyond (e.g. a 7B or 13B model on 12 GB GPU) it becomes very difficult without offloading.
Memory Optimization for Full FT: If choosing this path, use: - Mixed precision (FP16 or BF16) training to halve memory usage and increase speed. - Gradient Accumulation to simulate a larger batch if batch size is limited by memory. - Gradient Checkpointing to trade computation for memory by not storing all intermediate activations. This helps with deep models. - DeepSpeed ZeRO or Fully Sharded Data Parallel (FSDP) if multi-GPU or CPU offloading is available. For example, DeepSpeed ZeRO Stage 3 can offload optimizer states to CPU, allowing larger effective model size at cost of speed. - Accelerate with cpu_offload or disk_offload if only CPU RAM is available for overflow (useful if GPU memory is extremely limited, but slows training).
However, given the focus on minimal hardware, we strongly consider parameter-efficient fine-tuning below, which can dramatically reduce memory while achieving comparable performance.
### 4.2 Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT – e.g. LoRA, Adapters)
Instead of updating all 3B parameters, we insert small trainable modules or adapt a fraction of parameters. This approach keeps the original model weights mostly frozen and only learns a small number of new parameters (typically <1% of total).
LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation) is a popular PEFT method: - It adds learnable rank-decomposition matrices ($A$ and $B$ of low rank $r$) to existing weight matrices (usually the query/key/value projection in each self-attention layer). Only these $A$ and $B$ matrices (and perhaps a few biases) get trained. - The rest of the model remains fixed (thus frozen in memory, often loaded in 8-bit to save space). LoRA significantly reduces trainable parameters – e.g. under 0.5% of total for a 350M model, similar or less for a 3B model.

def run_prompt(prompt, model='gpt-3.5-turbo', temperature=0):
    response = openai.ChatCompletion.create(
        model=model,
        messages=[{'role':'user','content': prompt}],
        temperature=temperature)
    return response['choices'][0]['message']['content']

## 2. A/B Experiment Function

def ab_test(prompt_a, prompt_b, n=5):
    results = []
    for i in range(n):
        out_a = run_prompt(prompt_a)
        out_b = run_prompt(prompt_b)
        results.append({'trial': i, 'A': out_a, 'B': out_b})
    return results

import json, uuid, datetime, pathlib
def log_failure(prompt, input_text, output_text, issue):
    log = {
        'id': str(uuid.uuid4()),
        'timestamp': datetime.datetime.utcnow().isoformat(),
        'prompt': prompt,
        'input': input_text,
        'output': output_text,
        'issue': issue
    }
    pathlib.Path('failure_logs').mkdir(exist_ok=True)
    with open(f'failure_logs/{log["id"]}.json', 'w') as f:
        json.dump(log, f, indent=2)
    return log['id']

# AutoPrompt & OPRO: Automated Gradient‑Based Prompt Engineering
This notebook walks through two state‑of‑the‑art automated prompt discovery methods:
1. **AutoPrompt** – greedily inserts tokens that maximise a supervised objective.
2. **OPRO (One‑Prompt Reasoning Optimisation)** – searches for chain‑of‑thought prompts that maximise *reasoning* reward.

*Pedagogical goal:* Show how **model gradients** and **search/optimisation** can find high‑performing prompts without human intuition.

model_name = 'bert-base-uncased'

def prompt_accuracy(prompt_tokens):
    correct=0
    for ex in dataset:
        sent=ex['sentence']
        label=ex['label']
        text = tok.cls_token + ' ' + ' '.join(prompt_tokens) + ' ' + sent + ' It was ' + tok.mask_token + '.'
        inp = tok(text, return_tensors='pt')
        with torch.no_grad():
            logits = mlm(**inp).logits
        mask_ix = (inp['input_ids'][0]==tok.mask_token_id).nonzero()[0]
        probs = logits[0, mask_ix].softmax(-1)
        pred = probs[tok.convert_tokens_to_ids('great')] > probs[tok.convert_tokens_to_ids('terrible')]
        if pred.item() == label: correct +=1
    return correct/len(dataset)

import operator
from typing import List, Literal, Union, NamedTuple, Optional
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field

OperatorType = Literal["+", "-", "*", "/"]
TokenType = Union[float, OperatorType]

## We use these schemas to prompt the LLM to generate equations that evaluate to 24.


class Equation(BaseModel):
    """The formula combining the provided numbers to reach the target of 24."""

    tokens: List[TokenType] = Field(
        description="The stack of tokens and operators in reverse-polish notation. Example: [3, 4, '+', -1, '*'] would evaluate to (3 + 4) * -1 = -7.",
    )

    def compute(self) -> float:
        op_funcs = {
            "+": operator.add,
            "-": operator.sub,
            "*": operator.mul,
            "/": operator.truediv,
        }
        stack = []
        for token in self.tokens:
            if isinstance(token, float):
                stack.append(token)
            else:
                b, a = stack.pop(), stack.pop()
                stack.append(op_funcs[token](a, b))

        return stack[0]


class GuessEquations(BaseModel):
    """Submit multiple equations as guesses."""

    reasoning: str = Field(
        description="The reasoning behind the submitted guesses. Explain how you arrived at these equations."
    )

    equations: List[Equation] = Field(
        description="The list of equations to submit as guesses."
    )


## These objects will represent a single "candidate" (or scored candidate) within our agent's state.
# You can update the candidate object to match your own task.


class Candidate(NamedTuple):
    candidate: Equation
    score: Optional[float] = None
    feedback: Optional[str] = None

    def __str__(self):
        try:
            computed = self.candidate.compute()
        except Exception as e:
            computed = f"Invalid equation: {self.candidate.tokens}; Error: {repr(e)}"

        return f"Equation({self.candidate.tokens}) = {computed} (Reward: {self.score})"


class ScoredCandidate(Candidate):
    candidate: Equation
    score: float
    feedback: str

def compute_score(problem: str, candidate: Candidate) -> ScoredCandidate:
    numbers = list(map(int, problem.split()))
    # Check that the candidate equation uses all 4 numbers exactly once
    used_numbers = [
        token for token in candidate.candidate.tokens if isinstance(token, float)
    ]
    if sorted(used_numbers) != sorted(numbers):
        score = 0
        feedback = "The equation must use all 4 numbers exactly once."
        return ScoredCandidate(
            candidate=candidate.candidate, score=score, feedback=feedback
        )
    try:
        result = candidate.candidate.compute()
        score = 1 / (1 + abs(24 - result))
        feedback = f"Result: {result}"
    except Exception as e:
        score = 0
        feedback = f"Invalid equation. Error: {repr(e)}"
    return ScoredCandidate(
        candidate=candidate.candidate, score=score, feedback=feedback
    )

import operator
from typing import Optional, Dict, Any
from typing_extensions import Annotated, TypedDict
from langgraph.graph import StateGraph

from langchain_core.runnables import RunnableConfig
from langgraph.constants import Send
from langgraph.checkpoint.memory import MemorySaver


def update_candidates(
    existing: Optional[list] = None,
    updates: Optional[Union[list, Literal["clear"]]] = None,
) -> List[str]:
    if existing is None:
        existing = []
    if updates is None:
        return existing
    if updates == "clear":
        return []
    # Concatenate the lists
    return existing + updates


class ToTState(TypedDict):
    problem: str
    candidates: Annotated[List[Candidate], update_candidates]
    scored_candidates: Annotated[List[ScoredCandidate], update_candidates]
    depth: Annotated[int, operator.add]


class Configuration(TypedDict, total=False):
    max_depth: int
    threshold: float
    k: int
    beam_size: int


def _ensure_configurable(config: RunnableConfig) -> Configuration:
    """Get params that configure the search algorithm."""
    configurable = config.get("configurable", {})
    return {
        **configurable,
        "max_depth": configurable.get("max_depth", 10),
        "threshold": config.get("threshold", 0.9),
        "k": configurable.get("k", 5),
        "beam_size": configurable.get("beam_size", 3),
    }


class ExpansionState(ToTState):
    seed: Optional[Candidate]


def expand(state: ExpansionState, *, config: RunnableConfig) -> Dict[str, List[str]]:
    """Generate the next state."""
    configurable = _ensure_configurable(config)
    if not state.get("seed"):
        candidate_str = ""
    else:
        candidate_str = "\n\n" + str(state["seed"])
    try:
        equation_submission = solver.invoke(
            {
                "problem": state["problem"],
                "candidate": candidate_str,
                "k": configurable["k"],
            },
            config=config,
        )
    except Exception:
        return {"candidates": []}
    new_candidates = [
        Candidate(candidate=equation) for equation in equation_submission.equations
    ]
    return {"candidates": new_candidates}


def score(state: ToTState) -> Dict[str, List[float]]:
    """Evaluate the candidate generations."""
    candidates = state["candidates"]
    scored = []
    for candidate in candidates:
        scored.append(compute_score(state["problem"], candidate))
    return {"scored_candidates": scored, "candidates": "clear"}


def prune(
    state: ToTState, *, config: RunnableConfig
) -> Dict[str, List[Dict[str, Any]]]:
    scored_candidates = state["scored_candidates"]
    beam_size = _ensure_configurable(config)["beam_size"]
    organized = sorted(
        scored_candidates, key=lambda candidate: candidate[1], reverse=True
    )
    pruned = organized[:beam_size]
    return {
        # Update the starting point for the next iteration
        "candidates": pruned,
        # Clear the old memory
        "scored_candidates": "clear",
        # Increment the depth by 1
        "depth": 1,
    }


def should_terminate(
    state: ToTState, config: RunnableConfig
) -> Union[Literal["__end__"], Send]:
    configurable = _ensure_configurable(config)
    solved = state["candidates"][0].score >= configurable["threshold"]
    if solved or state["depth"] >= configurable["max_depth"]:
        return "__end__"
    return [
        Send("expand", {**state, "seed": candidate})
        for candidate in state["candidates"]
    ]


# Create the graph
builder = StateGraph(state_schema=ToTState, config_schema=Configuration)

# Add nodes
builder.add_node(expand)
builder.add_node(score)
builder.add_node(prune)

# Add edges
builder.add_edge("expand", "score")
builder.add_edge("score", "prune")
builder.add_conditional_edges("prune", should_terminate, path_map=["expand", "__end__"])

# Set entry point
builder.add_edge("__start__", "expand")

# Compile the graph
graph = builder.compile(checkpointer=MemorySaver())

**Purpose:** A guided skeleton to help you build a customized scheduling program for **your domain**

Markdown cell 4

## 1) Task schema & domain ideas

Each task is a **dict**:

```python
{
  "title": str,          # short label
  "type": str,           # category (e.g., "data", "modeling", "eval", "docs", "ops")
  "est_min": int,        # estimated minutes
  "importance": int,     # 1..5 (5 = must-do)
  # Optional:
  # "requires": ["other title", ...], # prerequisites if you want dependency logic
  # "notes": "anything helpful"
}
```

> **Data Science customization ideas**
- Use **types** like: `"data"`, `"eda"`, `"feature"`, `"modeling"`, `"eval"`, `"docs"`, `"ops"`, `"reading"`.
- Treat `"modeling"` blocks as **minimum 20–30 min** (don’t slice too small).
- After any `"modeling"` block, schedule a short `"eval"` or `"notes"` block to **review results**.
- Prioritize `"data"` tasks **before** `"modeling"` tasks (data readiness first).
- Round-robin across **modes** (`"reading" → "coding" → "analysis"`) to reduce fatigue.
- Boost importance for tasks with near **deadlines** or **compute bookings**.

from langchain.output_parsers import StrOutputParser

template1 = ChatPromptTemplate.from_messages([
    ("system", "You are a data retriever."),

Markdown cell 1
